text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Two of every three Swedes want to keep nuclear power station Barseback open despite a government plan to close one reactor next year and a second by 2001. A poll found a majority of Swedes do not want any closures before the general election in September 1998.

- Engineer Sandvik posted a worse-than-expected 21 percent drop in 1996 profit to 4.45 billion crowns and said it planned a share redemption in the wake of vehicle maker Volvo's plans. A share redemption gets around Swedish laws that do not permit a share buyback.

- There is no shortage of risk capital for new investment funds. Risk capital fund Industrikapital is currently seeking four to five billion crowns for the group's third fund, IK 97. Also Nordic Capital is planning a new fund.

- The criminal protection racket is becoming more widespread among Swedish shops, according to a retail industry association. The number of shop robberies increased by 30 percent last year and gave a sharp boost to the number of shops and restaurants paying not to be raided.
- Three members of the Riksbank's board say Sweden should join the European economic and monetary union (EMU) from the start in 1999 as the Riksbank itself has recommended.

- Swedish unemployment fell by 7,000 last week while the number of free jobs increased with the first three weeks of February showing as many free jobs as all of January, according to Labour Board statistics. But although the board said unemployment is decreasing it is only by nominal amounts.

- Sweden's government and industry leaders are in an angry public debate over the government's plans to start dismantling the country's nuclear energy plants next year. The business community has lost confidence in the government as a result of a series of actions which have worsened the business climate, according to a letter published in a Swedish newspaper at the weekend and signed by 101 prominent business leaders. Industry Minister Anders Sundstrom responded with a press release in which he decried the inability of corporate leaders to recognise positive signals in the business climate.
- Nearly a week before the merger of Foreningsbanken and Swebank someone calling himself PEO sent a message to several stock tip pages on the Internet accurately describing the deal.

- Swedish state-owned power company Vattenfall and Finnish counterpart IVO are both interested in buying Keski-Suomen Valo, a power company based in Jyvaskyla, Finland. The company, which is expected to command a purchase price of about two billion crowns, is presently owned by 22 Finnish companies.

- Tool and steel products maker Sandvik said fourth quarter pre-tax profit fell 31 percent as a stronger crown eroded the value of foreign-currency sales and steel prices fell. At the same time the company said it was considering buying back and cancelling shares worth four billion crowns.
